newsitem.title: USA: Crop insurance execs accused of corruption in Espy case.
newsitem.headline: Crop insurance execs accused of corruption in Espy case.

text.p: The two top officials of the nation's second largest crop insurer knowingly schemed to funnel illegal campaign contributions to the brother of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy to gain access to the Clinton cabinet member, government prosecutors charged on Tuesday.

Concluding the third trial stemming from the criminal probe of Espy being led by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz, prosecutors said that former Crop Growers Corp chairman John Hemmingson and senior vice president Gary Black concealed more than $40,000 in corporate contributions to Henry Espy, in order to win the favor of Mike Espy and fatten their wallets.
"This case is about corruption -- corruption of the political process," said prosecuting attorney Jacob Frenkel in presenting the government's closing arguments.

The government team charged that in 1993 and 1994 Hemmingson and Black were concerned about proposals to reform the nation's crop insurance system, and maintained that by gaining the favor of then Agriculture Secretary Espy, legislation was passed that was good for their company.
As major stockholders in the company, prosecutors said Hemmingson and Black then netted millions of dollars.
Defense attorneys argued that the government case lacked any proof, and said the defendents had a "good faith belief" that their actions were not illegal.
"They didn't think they were doing anything wrong," said Hemingson's attorney William Mauzy.
"The government has no evidence against my client," said Black's attorney Theodore Wells.

Black and Hemmingson have been charged with implementing an elaborate scheme to disguise $26,000 worth of corporate contributions to Henry Espy as individual contributions from employees, family members and other acquaintances.
They were also charged with funnelling a $20,000 corporate contribution to help retire Espy's campaign debt through a New Orleans lawyer.
Hemmingson has already been found guilty in a separate trial in New Orleans of money laundering of the $20,000 and of interstate transportation of the fraudulently obtained check.
Late last month the corporation of Crop Growers pleaded no contest to conspiring to defraud the Federal Election Commission and was fined $2 million.
Henry Espy unsuccessfully ran for his brother's congressional seat in 1993, after his brother Mike was appointed Agriculture Secretary in 1992.
Mike Espy resigned from the cabinet in late 1994 amid allegations that he had illegally accepted gifts and favors from companies his agency was in charge of regulating.

Smaltz's probe has brought criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns and the conviction of the largest fruit cooperative in the nation for fraud and illegal gratuities to Mike Espy.
The more than two-year probe of Espy is widely expected to lead to the indictment this year of the former cabinet member.

Government investigators have also conducted an agressive probe into the relationship between Espy and Tyson Foods Inc, the Arkansas-based poultry giant, and legal experts said an indictment of the poultry company is not unlikely. Tyson's chairman Don Tyson has long had close ties to President Bill Clinton, former Arkansas governnor.
